name: Unusual Machines, Inc.

profile.description: Unusual Machines, Inc. is an Orlando, Florida-based maker of NDAA-compliant drone components and subsystems, including motors, flight controllers, cameras, and FPV goggles. It also sells consumer FPV gear through its Fat Shark and Rotor Riot brands. The company has shifted from retail hobby sales to enterprise and defense customers, which made up about 95% of Q2 2026 revenue of $16.7M (up 687% YoY). It has a pending acquisition of Upgrade Energy. CEO Allan Evans leads the company, and Donald Trump Jr. serves as an advisor and shareholder.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): After acquiring Fat Shark and Rotor Riot in 2024, UMAC moved from retail FPV hobby gear to supplying domestic, NDAA-compliant components to drone OEMs. That opened a new revenue stream: enterprise customers were about 95% of Q2 2026 revenue of $16.7M, up 687% YoY [1][2]. AI Deployment (0/2): We found no AI-powered products or quantified AI savings. UMAC supplies motors, controllers, and optics, not autonomy software [3]. Market Share (1/2): UMAC is a leading U.S. source of non-Chinese FPV components and benefits from DJI restrictions, but it is a small, meaningful player without published share data, and its largest customer is about 42% of revenue [1][2]. Pipeline (1/2): Management gave internal targets of $12-14M for Q3 and $25M for Q4 and expects Drone Dominance program demand. These are revenue targets, not named next-generation products with launch dates [2]. R&D Intensity (0/1): We found no evidence of above-peer R&D spending.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): The mission to rebuild an American drone component supply chain independent of China is clear and timely, and the company has backed it with domestic motor manufacturing. It has not yet been tested by time or proven through execution [3]. Community Impact (0/2): We found no charitable or community investment programs. Employee Retention (0/2): The company had only three employees in 2023 and has scaled rapidly through acquisitions, so there is no tenure or retention data [3]. Insider Buying (0/2): Insider sentiment is net negative. Examples include an executive's 150,000-share sale and a director's filing to sell 500,000 shares (about $14.8M) in mid-2025, and the company has kept issuing stock, including $60M through its ATM in Q2 2026 [1][4].

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Scored mechanically as a Growth stock: 2.0 of 6 available weighted points, which rounds to 3. The 5-year revenue CAGR is excluded because revenue was effectively zero before the 2024 acquisitions, and Forward PEG is excluded because earnings are negative. D/E of 0.8% (1.00) and TTM revenue growth of 687% (1.00) meet target [5]. ROE of -2.9% (0.00, double weight), a profit margin of -20.3% (0.00), and a negative Forward P/E of -78.5 (0.00) all score zero [5]. Q2 2026 brought a GAAP net loss of about $7.8M on a 34.7% gross margin, against about $229.6M of cash [1]. Liquidity is about $59M per day.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): UMAC makes physical drone hardware (motors, flight controllers, cameras) that is in short supply. Management says the market is supply-constrained through at least 2027, and AI-enabled autonomous drones raise demand for the components UMAC sells [2]. Analyst coverage focuses on defense procurement, customer concentration, and political risk, not AI substitution [4][6]. AI Opportunity (0/1): UMAC reports no revenue from AI products or services.

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, Unusual Machines has the start of a real cause, domestic drone supply-chain independence, but the company is too young and too driven by policy and capital-market events to show infinite-game behavior. Its stock has repeatedly moved on political news (the Trump Jr. advisory role, the DJI ban, government-stake speculation) more than on operations. Heavy ATM dilution and insider selling point to a short time horizon.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Rebuilding an American drone component industrial base is distinctive and service-oriented. Leadership consistently refers to it and has backed it with a domestic motor plant in Orlando [2][3]. It has not yet been tested through a downturn or a leadership transition.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Choosing higher-cost U.S. manufacturing over cheaper Chinese sourcing, and shifting away from the original retail hobby base toward enterprise and defense, both carried near-term cost [1][3]. Raising capital opportunistically at elevated share prices, however, follows a finite capital-markets playbook.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): The company has grown from three employees in 2023 through acquisitions, so there has been no time to build a proven culture. Steady insider selling also undercuts any signal of a shared long-term commitment [3][4].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): UMAC has repositioned from consumer FPV retail to defense and enterprise components, and enterprise is now about 95% of revenue. It is also expanding into power systems through the pending Upgrade Energy acquisition [1][2]. This is a meaningful pivot, though driven by market opportunity.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): The company's competitive framing is defined against Chinese suppliers such as DJI and relies on policy-driven exclusion, not on learning from rivals [3][6].

investment_thesis: Unusual Machines is a direct beneficiary of the U.S. push to remove Chinese components from military and enterprise drones. Q2 2026 revenue of $16.7M rose 687% YoY and 106% sequentially, and management targets $25M in Q4 2026, excluding the Upgrade Energy acquisition [1][2]. With about $229.6M of cash, essentially no debt (0.8% D/E), and a market it says is supply-constrained through 2027, UMAC can fund domestic capacity while Drone Dominance program demand ramps [1][2][5].
thesis_continued: The bear case is concentration, losses, and political risk. One customer was about 42% of Q2 revenue, the company lost $7.8M in Q2, and management expects gross margin (34.7%) to dip in Q3 [1][2]. The stock's moves have been closely tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s advisory role, and an August 2026 House inquiry into his venture firm cut market-implied odds of a U.S. government equity stake from 45% to 26% [4][6]. Ongoing ATM issuance ($60M in Q2) and insider selling dilute shareholders.
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results against the internal $12-14M revenue target, and progress toward $25M in Q4 as Drone Dominance orders begin
Closing the Upgrade Energy acquisition, adding power-system content per drone
Further DJI and Chinese component restrictions pushing U.S. drone OEMs toward NDAA-compliant domestic suppliers
key_risks: Customer concentration: the largest customer was about 42% of Q2 2026 revenue, so one order slip could miss the $25M Q4 target
Political and reputational risk from Trump Jr. ties: congressional scrutiny and ethics concerns could affect Pentagon contracting and valuation
Persistent GAAP losses (-20% profit margin) and repeated ATM equity raises diluting shareholders, with net insider selling

backlog.note: UMAC does not disclose backlog or book-to-bill. Management describes demand as exceeding supply through at least 2027 and gives internal targets of $12-14M (Q3) and $25M (Q4 2026), but without a disclosed funded order book the signal is held at yellow pending verification.
